Rules / Modernization

SK1062 Use the string literal form that needs no escapes

An escaped or verbatim literal a raw string would write without escapes, a raw string whose delimiter is longer than it needs to be, or an escape sequence that is simply a character.

CategoryModernization
Default severityhint
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floor—
Since1.3

Why

Escape-dense literals — Windows paths, embedded JSON, regexes — are where a stray backslash changes the meaning of the string and nothing says so. "\\d+\\.\\d+" and "{\"id\":1}" have to be decoded by the reader before they can be checked against whatever they are supposed to match, and the decoding is where the mistake gets made. A raw string removes the escaping entirely, and the shortest correct delimiter is the one that says the content has no quotes to worry about.

Example

Instead of:

var pattern = "\\d+\\.\\d+";
var body = @"{""id"":1}";
var tag = "\x41";

Write:

var pattern = """\d+\.\d+""";
var body = """{"id":1}""";
var tag = "A";

When it does not fire

⚠ The delimiter is the rule and getting it wrong emits code that does not compile. A single-line raw string's fence is the longest run of quotes in the content plus one, never fewer than three, and its content may not begin or end with a quote at all. Rather than trusting that arithmetic, every replacement this rule proposes is re-parsed as an expression and its value compared against the original's before the finding is reported — a wrong fence cannot become a diagnostic, let alone a fix. ⚠ Only single-line forms are touched. A value containing a newline, a tab, or any other control character has no single-line raw spelling, and a multi-line raw string carries indentation rules that make the rewrite a formatting decision rather than a mechanical one. ⚠ Version-gated per shape, not per rule. The three raw-string shapes are silent below C# 11; simplifying an escape sequence to the character it denotes has no floor at all, and a single rule-level floor would have silenced it on every older project. ⚠ \x is variable-length and greedy — "\x41B" is one escape denoting U+041B, not \x41 followed by B — so the scan consumes it the way the lexer does and then declines it, because the character is outside the printable ASCII range the shape admits. \\, \", \n, \r, \t, \0 and \U are never simplified. ⚠ A literal inside an interpolation hole is left alone: SK1063 has its own opinion about those, and two rules rewriting one span is one of them being wrong. ⚠ `UseVerbatimString` is not covered — this rule goes to the raw form and never produces a verbatim one, and crediting an inspection whose output it does not reproduce would overstate the parity.
